newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: East China Sea islands sovereignty row.
newsitem.headline: East China Sea islands sovereignty row.

text.p: Lurking in the background of a Japan-China-Taiwan sovereignty row is the possibility the East China Sea islands all three claim may be rich in oil and gas, but industry sources said on Wednesday there are no proven reserves in the area.

"There is some expectation that there may be hydrocarbon resources," said Hisanori Gotoh, deputy director of the petroleum exploration division of Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry.
"The chances make it fairly interesting in that governments are interested in territorial rights," he said. "The situation is not unsimilar to the Falklands."
"We have not conducted any exploration," Gotoh added. "Of course we have to do drilling or tests before it is proved, but we are hopeful there will be oil or gas."
However, Gotoh said there were no government plans to explore the disputed area.
Sources close to state-owned China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) and Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corporation (CPC) confirmed that no exploration had been undertaken.

"There is no firm evidence that there could be hydrocarbons. The islands have not been properly explored," said Stuart Saint, vice-president of analyst Arthur D. Little in Singapore. "The proper way is to do seismic studies, but these have not been done."
China, Japan, and Taiwan all claim soverignty over the tiny islands, called the Diaoyus in Chinese and Senkakus in Japanese.

Japan has refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion. Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
The long-dormant dispute over the uninhabited islands flared in July when a rightist Japanese group built a lighthouse and a war memorial on the islands to bolster Tokyo's sovereignty claim.
Although China has not taken any action, last week it called on Japan to stop encouraging the rightist activities or risk escalating the dispute.

Taiwan has been more vocal, demanding that Japan remove the lighthouse. Earlier this month, Japanese coast guard ships barred private Taiwanese boats from entering the area while the rightist group repaired the typhoon-damaged structure.
Taiwan has said it expects to hold talks with Japan in early October to discuss fishing rights in the disputed area.

"The area is more crucial for the fishing industry because there are fish there," said a Chinese source involved in offshore drilling. "There is probably a lot of oil under the islands but China has not done any exploration, or rather cannot do any until the highly sensitive political situation is sorted out."

All three countries are dependent on oil imports. Last year, China produced around 3 million barrels-per-day (bpd) of oil while consuming 3.3 million bpd. In 1995, Japan had to import 4.6 million bpd of crude oil and used 5.8 million bpd.
Taiwan has to import oil for two refineries that produce about 720,000 bpd of crude products.
"If the areas were made available, there would be companies interested ... but serious investment will be dependent on the technical information," said Saint.

Analysts said the island dispute was also awkward for CNOOC and CPC in the wake of their unprecedented agreement in July to explore jointly for oil and gas in an area off south China's Pearl River delta.
